overview: Assyria grew from its northern Mesopotamian heartland into an empire extending through much of the Near East. This card emphasizes its Middle and Neo-Assyrian phases. The imported map repeats a small core outline and greatly understates the later empire. Its 1500 to 500 BCE display interval is not the monarchy’s lifespan: royal rule ended around 609 BCE.

periods.title: Expansion and contraction
periods.summary: Middle Assyrian kings expanded; territory later contracted.

periods.title: The Neo-Assyrian empire
periods.summary: Renewed expansion created a far-reaching imperial state.

items.text: In the fourteenth century BCE, Ashur-uballit I recovered productive lands around Nineveh and Arbela. Later Middle Assyrian kings expanded westward and into Babylonia. Tukulti-Ninurta I established a new royal city across the Tigris from Ashur. Expansion was uneven: Assyrian territory contracted again near the end of the second millennium BCE.

Assyrian rulers forcibly relocated people from conquered regions. Moving communities weakened local leaders and supplied workers for building and farming elsewhere. This policy could make deportees dependent on imperial officials for their survival. The empire’s many languages therefore reflected both movement between regions and the human cost of conquest.

A guardian bull from Ashurnasirpal II’s palace at Nimrud has a human head, wings and five legs. Seen from the front, it stands firmly; from the side, it strides. The extra leg solved an artistic problem rather neatly. Such lamassu guarded important palace entrances and helped make royal buildings feel imposing.

sections.title: Meals, bathrooms and life around the palace

items.text: The Northwest Palace at Nimrud housed the royal family and domestic staff in its southern part. Several courtyards had wells. Room ZZ contained kitchen benches, a bread oven and cooking vessels. Behind the enormous ceremonial rooms, somebody still had to fetch water, prepare food and get a meal ready.

Assyrian palace bathing rooms used water-resistant floors and drains connected to underground channels. At Nimrud, surviving installations include a drain and a covered access opening. Some arrangements may have supported perishable toilet fittings. Researchers also interpret certain drain plugs as barriers against smells and animals. Archaeologists have the plumbing, but must reconstruct some of what stood above it.

At Ziyaret Tepe, ancient Tushan, excavators found the equipment of everyday work: weights, seals and accounting tokens, alongside spindle whorls, a fragment of an ivory comb and bronze pins. Knucklebones suggest games as well. A frontier provincial city contained offices and workshops, but its inhabitants also dressed, groomed themselves and found time to play.

A clay tablet from Tushan lists women attached to the palace administration. Researchers identified 144 name entries, with 59 still legible. Many names did not fit the familiar languages they compared. One proposal connects them with deported women from western Iran, but their precise language and origin remain uncertain. Even an office list can preserve traces of people otherwise missing from history.

Around thirty bread-and-wine lists from eighth-century BCE Kalhu list people receiving provisions, including court scholars. Their order and allocations reveal differences in status. Researchers debate whether these were ordinary rations or extra distributions for special occasions. The lists let us glimpse who received food at court, without supplying a complete menu for every Assyrian household.

Sennacherib’s inscription on the Jerwan aqueduct describes collecting water from rivers and mountain springs for a canal reaching the Nineveh plain. It says a white-limestone aqueduct carried the flow across deep valleys. Moving water over an obstacle required organized construction as well as a royal command: the stream could not simply be told to climb uphill.

More than 30,000 clay tablets from Nineveh survive in the British Museum’s collection. They include fragments and material from different collections, not that many complete books from one room. Ownership notes help researchers identify Ashurbanipal’s library. Other notes reveal copying and editing, allowing modern scholars to investigate who assembled this enormous collection of knowledge.

Scribal training placed great emphasis on memorizing and recalling texts. Scholars also kept collections at home and in temples. One healer explained to King Esarhaddon that he needed to consult a writing-board at his house to answer a question about an earthquake ritual. Even an expert sometimes had to go and look it up.

The medical writings associated with Ashurbanipal’s library often begin with symptoms, then give ingredients and instructions for preparing and administering treatments. Some add a prognosis. Rituals and incantations appear alongside these practical recipes. Researchers reconstruct the medical collection by joining and comparing broken tablets, recovering how ancient specialists organized care rather than assuming that every remedy worked.

sections.title: A written sample and life after conquest

items.text: The Jerwan inscription contains “MAN ŠÚ MAN KUR aš-šur”, translated “king of the world, king of Assyria”. This is the edition’s scholarly transliteration of Akkadian cuneiform, not the original wedge shapes or a pronunciation guide. The phrase introduces Sennacherib on stone blocks from his aqueduct, dated broadly to his reign, 704 to 681 BCE.

Conquest did not empty every Assyrian city. The Red House at Dur-Katlimmu, an elite residence with red-painted interiors, remained occupied beyond the fall of Nineveh. Four Assyrian cuneiform texts there use dates from Nebuchadnezzar II’s Babylonian reign. Much of the house burned around the middle of the sixth century BCE, giving this particular building a history longer than the empire’s.

ending.text: The Babylonian Chronicle records Ashur’s capture in 614 BCE and Nineveh’s destruction in 612. The remaining Assyrian royal force lost Harran and failed to recover it in 609. The last king then disappears from the surviving written record. Imperial rule ended, while occupation and Assyrian writing continued in places such as the Red House at Dur-Katlimmu.
